自動豎琴一詞見於1881年12月10日齊默曼申請、1882年5月9日核發的美國專: The term autoharp appears in US patent 257808, applied for by Zimmerman on 10 December 1881 and granted on 9 May 1882, the earliest patent for a zither with a mechanical damping device for making chords. The first form was trapezoidal with sideways damping; vertical chord bars came later, and the instrument was shown at the World's Industrial and Cotton Centenary Exposition of 1884–1885. On 20 May 1884 Lindemann and Gutt applied for German patent 29930, granted on 5 January 1885, with a different mechanical realisation. The complete British specification of 11 March 1885 used vertical bars and added picks, and its outward form matched Zimmerman's small instrument; the name was registered as a trademark in 1893 and later became a generic term.
自動豎琴屬弦鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs 編號 314.122-5。: The autoharp is a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 314.122-5. The source records a wooden body whose soundboard usually has guitar-style soundholes and may be solid or laminated; the top and the slanted side carry a pin block of laminated wood, with tuning pins like those of a piano or a concert zither. At the other end the strings are held by metal pins or a grooved metal plate. The chord bars are plastic, wood or metal, faced with felt or foam damping pads on the string side and with wooden, plastic or rubber feet behind. The sounding bodies are the strings; the string material is not stated.

Its range is wide, spanning three to four octaves: the treble is crisp and clear, the middle register full and round, the bass steady and mellow. The soundbox gives the tone a natural reverberance, and it projects well. Compared with the guzheng the autoharp is lighter and softer; compared with the guitar it has an added folk gentleness. What sets it apart is that the chord-bar mechanism produces rich harmony, so that a single strum yields a full multi-part sound. Its tone is at once traditional and modern, keeping the warmth of an old string instrument and the clarity of a modern one.

The autoharp is a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 314.122-5, and a member of the zither family. Its distinguishing feature is a set of chord bars with damping pads that, when pressed, silence the strings not in the chosen chord. To play, one hand presses the relevant chord bar against the strings while the other strums. Modern instruments commonly have thirty-six strings, with larger numbers and sets of twelve, fifteen or twenty-one chord bars, and can play major, minor and dominant seventh chords. Two-key or three-key diatonic versions can be used at campfires or festivals to accompany the fiddle.
